name: Theoretical yield
seoDesc: Theoretical yield: work out molecular weight (Limiting reagent) from the mass and the stoichiometry. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units…
summary: molecular weight (Limiting reagent) is what the Theoretical yield calculator works out, and it gets there from the mass, the stoichiometry, the moles and the theoretical yield. That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Theoretical yield calculator work?
sections.html:
The Theoretical yield calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports molecular weight (Limiting reagent) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the mass, the stoichiometry (Desired product), the moles (Desired product) and the theoretical yield.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Theoretical yield calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Molecular weight=mass ÷ moles
Moles=moles × stoichiometry ÷ stoichiometry
Molecular weight=theoretical yield ÷ moles

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Mass = 10 g and Moles = 10 mol. The calculator returns Molecular weight = 1 g/mol.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Molecular weight = 1 g/mol should be roughly the size you expected from Mass = 10 g and Moles = 10 mol.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in grams per mole, and convertible to any of the 4 units on that chip.
  • Shown in moles, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in grams per mole, and convertible to any of the 4 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in grams
  • Molar mass, opening in grams per mole
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Molar mass, opening in grams per mole
  • Mass, opening in grams

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Theoretical yield calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the mass, the stoichiometry and the moles — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Theoretical yield calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns molecular weight (Limiting reagent), derived from the mass, the stoichiometry and the moles. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Theoretical yield calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mass, the stoichiometry, the moles and the theoretical yield, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass opens in grams and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Molecular weight = 1 g/mol. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Theoretical yield calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
